newsitem.title: USA: Dollar gains as market prepares for possible rate hike.
newsitem.headline: Dollar gains as market prepares for possible rate hike.

text.p: The dollar was propelled higher against the German mark on Monday as traders bet that Federal Reserve policy-makers will raise short-term interest rates at their much-anticipated meeting on Tuesday .

The dollar also benefited from mark weakness against other European currencies and speculative buyers who bid the dollar back up against the Japanese yen after the U.S. currency tumbled sharply on news that Japan's international trade surplus jumped in April.
The dollar rose to 1.7080 marks by the end of trading from 1.6925 at Friday's close but closed nearly unchanged at 115.75 yen, compared with 115.70.

Trade was slow as most European markets were closed due to the Pentecost holiday, allowing market attention to fixate on the probability of U.S. central bankers raising official interest rates on Tuesday in an attempt to contain inflation.

Fed officials hiked interest rates for the first time in more than two years on March 25 to rein in the economy, but Wall Street remains divided on whether a second move is necessary given signs of economic slowdown in recent April data.

A Reuters poll on Monday showed that 21 of 39 primary dealers -- large banks that act as an intermediary between the Treasury Department and government security markets -- expect rates to remain unchanged.

"Tuesday's meeting is the big focus of the market. The consensus is fairly even at about 50/50 as to whether the Fed will do anything," said Dennis Pettit, foreign exchange manager at Long Term Credit Bank of Japan in New York.
"My thoughts are perhaps tht there's not sufficient political cover for them to raise rates tomorrow and that they might defer until July," Pettit added.
Remarks from Bundesbank board member Edgar Meister exacerbated the mark's weakness against the British pound, Italian lira and yen, thus aiding the dollar, dealers said.

Meister sparked concern that criteria for membership in Europe's planned single currency may be relaxed, which in turn would enable more countries to qualify and possibly weaken the resulting single currency.

Meister said Germany's recent efforts to recover an 18 billion mark tax revenue shortfall to meet qualifications shows how "thorny" meeting the single-currency criteria is for Germany, as well as most other European nations.

"It's not really a strong dollar, but a depreciating mark and appreciating pound against the mark, which has propelled the dollar higher against the mark," said John Nelson, foreign exchange trading manager at ABN-AMRO Bank.

The lira gained against the mark on expectations of an interest rate cut in the near future as the Bank of Italy lowered its repurchase rate to a historic low of 6.78 percent. Sterling was buoyed by better-than-expected UK public sector debt data.
The dollar dipped to a session low of 114.85 yen after Japan's Finance Ministry reported its customs-cleared trade surplus more than doubled in April from a year earlier to 831.48 billion yen.
The trade surplus with the United States, often a source of friction, surged 174.1 percent in April from a year earlier to 468.97 billion yen.
In other trading, the dollar rose to 1.4265 Swiss francs from 1.4200 and fell to Canadian $1.3713 from C$1.3733. Sterling rose to $1.6400 from $1.6365.
